problem: Twelve students from an olympiad class form two teams of six players each to play soccer every day after math class. Each day, they form two different teams from those formed on previous days. By the end of the year, each group of five students has played together on the same team exactly once. How many different teams were formed throughout the year?

answer_text:
# Finding the Number of Teams Formed

## Setting Up the Counting Problem

I have 12 students, and each day they're split into two teams of 6. The key condition is:

> **Every group of 5 students has played together on the same team exactly once.**

This means I need to count how many 6-person teams (blocks) are needed so that every 5-person subset is contained in **exactly one** team.

## Counting 5-Subsets

The total number of distinct groups of 5 students from 12 is:

$$\binom{12}{5} = \frac{12 \times 11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8}{5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 792$$

## Counting 5-Subsets Per Team

A single team of 6 players contains exactly:

$$\binom{6}{5} = 6$$

distinct groups of 5 players.

## Computing the Number of Teams

Since each 5-subset must appear on **exactly one** team, and each team "covers" exactly 6 different 5-subsets, the total number of teams is:

$$\frac{\binom{12}{5}}{\binom{6}{5}} = \frac{792}{6} = 132$$

## Verification of Consistency

- Each team has 6 members, so it generates 6 five-player groups ✓
- 132 teams × 6 five-subsets each = 792 = $\binom{12}{5}$ ✓
- Each day produces 2 complementary teams, giving 66 days ✓
- Each player appears in $\binom{11}{4}/\binom{5}{4} = 330/5 = 66$ teams, which is consistent with the 66-day schedule ✓

This structure is known as the **Steiner system S(5, 6, 12)**, and all the necessary divisibility conditions are satisfied, confirming the design exists.

## Answer

$$\boxed{132}$$
